notes.headline: Alcon: core EPS up 15% on wider margins, but cataract-lens sales slip in the US under competitive pressure; shares fall 4%
notes.takeaway: Sales rose 5% to $2.7 billion and core EPS 15% to $0.91, ahead of the $0.89 consensus, as the core operating margin widened to 21.8%. Implantable lens sales fell 2% on US competition and Alcon tightened its 2026 outlook to about 6% sales growth, and the shares fell 3.6%.
results: Alcon reported net sales of $2,717 million for the third quarter, up 5% on both a reported and constant-currency basis. Diluted EPS was $0.54, up 13%, and core diluted EPS, which excludes amortisation and one-off items, was $0.91, up 15%. The core operating margin rose to 21.8% from 20.2%.

Surgical sales rose 4% to $1,480 million. Implantables, mainly intraocular lenses used in cataract surgery, fell 2% to $422 million because of competitive pressure in the US, partly offset by the PanOptix Pro lens and international growth; consumables rose 6% and equipment 11% on the Unity surgical platform and the Valeda device. Vision care rose 6% to $1,237 million, with contact lenses up 5% in constant currency and ocular health, including eye drops, up 8%.
For nine months sales rose 7% to $8.2 billion and core EPS 14% to $2.60. Operating cash flow was $1,689 million and free cash flow $1,345 million, and Alcon returned $748 million to shareholders.
mgmt: Chief executive David Endicott said Alcon remains on track for its 2026 objectives, with six percent sales growth and double-digit core EPS growth year to date despite some specific areas of competitive pressure, and that momentum in new products, the pipeline and the acquisition of Neurotech Pharmaceuticals, which strengthens its retina portfolio, position it for sustainable long-term growth.

Alcon tightened its 2026 outlook to sales growth of about 6% in constant currency (from 5% to 7%), core operating margin expansion of 100 to 150 basis points (from 90 to 190) and core EPS growth of 12% to 14% (from 12% to 15%). It expects a net tariff impact of about $40 million for the year and assumes its markets grow about 3%.
view: Alcon is the global leader in eye care and one of the steadiest businesses in medical technology: an ageing population needs cataract surgery, contact lens wearers buy every month, and surgeons trained on Alcon equipment tend to stay with Alcon consumables. Against that backdrop, this was a solid quarter with one flaw. Margin expansion of 1.6 points and 15% core EPS growth show the company converting modest sales growth into strong profit growth, which is exactly what investors want from a mature medtech company.

The flaw is the US lens business. Intraocular lenses are Alcon’s highest-profile product, and a 1% decline while the market grows indicates share loss, most likely to Johnson & Johnson’s and Bausch & Lomb’s newer premium lenses. Management’s phrase about specific areas of competitive pressure is an acknowledgement. The narrowing of the guidance ranges, removing the top end of EPS growth, is a mild negative, and it explains the share-price reaction more than the quarter itself.

The bigger strategic move is into drugs. Neurotech brings an implant-based therapy for a degenerative retinal disease, continuing Alcon’s push into pharmaceutical eye care alongside its dry-eye franchise. It diversifies Alcon away from the surgical cycle, but pharmaceutical development carries regulatory and commercial risks that a device company has less experience managing. At around 21 times core earnings, the shares price Alcon as a quality compounder but no longer at a premium; regaining momentum in US lenses would restore confidence that the compounding can continue.
notes.watch: Watch US intraocular-lens trends and new premium lens launches, the margin path toward 2027, integration of Neurotech, and the tariff impact on costs.
